					<description><![CDATA[<p>Aggressive prediction of $1T by 2030 was $700B too low. Here's why. </p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/tsmc-oip-chip-industry-growth-blows-past-forecast/">TSMC OIP: Chip Industry Growth Blows Past Forecast</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>TSMC presented company and semiconductor industry updates at its Open Innovation Partners North America Technology Symposium last week. In January 2024, TSMC’s Kevin Zhang presented the slide below (see figure 1) for the Semiconductor Industry Outlook at ISSCC. It projected what then seemed like a bold forecast for worldwide semiconductor revenue to reach ~$1T by 2030.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" fetchpriority="high" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24282059" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Picture1.png?resize=1248%2C704&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="1248" height="704" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Picture1.png?w=1248&amp;ssl=1 1248w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Picture1.png?resize=300%2C169&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Picture1.png?resize=1024%2C578&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Picture1.png?resize=768%2C433&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Picture1.png?resize=600%2C338&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><br />
<strong>Fig. 1: 2024 semiconductor industry outlook forecast. Source: TSMC</strong></p>
<p>At this year’s OIC, TSMC North America CEO Sajiv Dalal said the Semiconductor Industry will hit ~1.7T by end of year, with &gt; $1T for AI alone. Dalal’s forecast is also in line with <a href="https://www.semiconductor-digest.com/gartner-forecasts-worldwide-semiconductor-revenue-to-reach-1-6-trillion-in-2026/">Gartner’s forecast</a> of ~$1.6T for the industry in 2026. This is an incredible leap on top of what originally seemed like an ambitious forecast. The surge in AI semiconductor spending has been accelerating at a ferocious pace.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24282060" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/tsmc2.png?resize=1248%2C701&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="1248" height="701" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/tsmc2.png?w=1248&amp;ssl=1 1248w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/tsmc2.png?resize=300%2C169&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/tsmc2.png?resize=1024%2C575&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/tsmc2.png?resize=768%2C431&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/tsmc2.png?resize=600%2C337&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><br />
<strong>Fig. 2: TSMC revenue forecast. Source: TSMC</strong></p>
<p>The slide shown above in Figure 2. shows revenue layered on top of TSMC technology and product milestones. The AI era portion highlights the current accelerated growth in revenue.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24282061" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/table1.png?resize=1248%2C264&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="1248" height="264" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/table1.png?w=1248&amp;ssl=1 1248w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/table1.png?resize=300%2C63&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/table1.png?resize=1024%2C217&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/table1.png?resize=768%2C162&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/table1.png?resize=600%2C127&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><br />
<strong>Table 1: TSMC August 2026 Revenue Update. Source: TSMC</strong></p>
<p>TSMC’s recent revenue numbers, shown in Table 1, show a 53.3% year-over-year increase and, for comparable January-to-August numbers for 2025 and 2026, a whopping 39.3% increase.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24282062" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/tsmc3.png?resize=1248%2C701&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="1248" height="701" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/tsmc3.png?w=1248&amp;ssl=1 1248w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/tsmc3.png?resize=300%2C169&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/tsmc3.png?resize=1024%2C575&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/tsmc3.png?resize=768%2C431&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/tsmc3.png?resize=600%2C337&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><br />
<strong>Fig. 3: Advanced nodes to support AI. Source: TSMC</strong></p>
<p>Figure 3 shows projected growth across HPC/mobile, auto and IoT segments. Li-Pen Yuan, vice president of business development at TSMC, said the number of new tape-outs (NTOs) had increased by 4× as measured by the second year of a new technology across the N5, N3 and N2 technologies. This is a massive acceleration in the number of new designs targeted for the N2 technology, which continues beyond N3’s increased new design rate.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24282067" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-28-at-3.31.56-PM.png?resize=1838%2C1028&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="1838" height="1028" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-28-at-3.31.56-PM.png?w=1838&amp;ssl=1 1838w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-28-at-3.31.56-PM.png?resize=300%2C168&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-28-at-3.31.56-PM.png?resize=1024%2C573&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-28-at-3.31.56-PM.png?resize=768%2C430&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-28-at-3.31.56-PM.png?resize=1536%2C859&amp;ssl=1 1536w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-28-at-3.31.56-PM.png?resize=600%2C336&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><br />
<strong>Fig. 4: AI scaling challenges. Source: TSMC</strong></p>
<p>The AI build-out increasingly makes new demands on compute, memory density, and power, as is shown in the projections for industry in figure 4. L.C. Lu, TSMC senior fellow and vice president for design and technology platforms, said inference token usage has grown 500× over the past three years and that inference is becoming the growth driver for AI.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24282064" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/tsmc5.png?resize=1248%2C696&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="1248" height="696" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/tsmc5.png?w=1248&amp;ssl=1 1248w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/tsmc5.png?resize=300%2C167&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/tsmc5.png?resize=1024%2C571&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/tsmc5.png?resize=768%2C428&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/tsmc5.png?resize=600%2C335&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><br />
<strong>Fig. 5: Power efficiency scaling. Source: TSMC</strong></p>
<p>Lu noted that power scaling extends Moore’s Law. For TSMC’s A14 Nanoflex, the cell height goes to 1.5× (vs. 2× for previous nodes), with a14% improvement in speed and 23% reduction in power versus N2P. Figure 5, above, shows HPC cell power efficiency improvements of 2.3× when going from N3P to A12 SPR.</p>
<p>For memory, Lu presented a figure of merit based on the number of transistors × speed@power. (#Trans × speed@Power). This benchmark will increase by 87× in 2029, based on predicted improvements from technology advancements. In five years, bandwidths for HBM will increase 34×, 3D DRAM 115×, and SRAM by 830×. The 2029 forecasts for energy/bit are SRAM 0.32pJ/bit, 3DDRAM 1pj/Bit, and HBM 2.5pJ/bit.</p>
<p>In an article covering the 2024 TSMC OIP,<a href="https://semiengineering.com/tsmcs-plan-for-closing-the-communication-gap/">TSMC’s Plan For Closing The Communication Gap</a>, the introduction of TSMC’s COUPE was discussed as an important milestone for TSMC to enable energy-efficient high-speed communication as serial data rates jump to 224G and 448G. TSMC-COUPE addresses the need for higher bandwidth with lower energy per bit.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24282065" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/tsmc6.png?resize=1248%2C701&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="1248" height="701" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/tsmc6.png?w=1248&amp;ssl=1 1248w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/tsmc6.png?resize=300%2C169&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/tsmc6.png?resize=1024%2C575&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/tsmc6.png?resize=768%2C431&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/tsmc6.png?resize=600%2C337&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><br />
<strong>Fig. 6: TSMC-COUPE scaling. Source: TSMC</strong></p>
<p>Figure 6 shows the future roadmap for TSMC-COUPE, including serial data rate increases in gigabits per second (Gbps). The ability to incorporate multiple wavelengths per fiber increases the overall bandwidth capacity of the fiber, as each wavelength is a carrier of high-speed data.</p>
<p>AI is now acting in a positive feedback environment, where advances in AI are leading to new tools and productivity in the development of new AI technologies. Greg Dix, vice president of engineering for Broadcom&#8217;s ASIC Products Division, said from project kick-off to tape-out of OpenAI’s Jalapeno custom AI ASIC was accomplished in just nine months. Dix noted that, in his view, the SoC era is ending and SiP is accelerating.</p>
<p>In new partnerships, Yuan noted that TSMC recently added imec as a partner, and IC-Link by imec received a partner of the year award following IC-Link&#8217;s integration into the OIP Cloud Alliance as its first managed-cloud service supporting mixed-partner EDA workflows. Amazon Web Services (AWS) and Microsoft Azure also were winners in this category. The TSMC EDA partners of the year awards went to Cadence, Siemens EDA and Synopsys.</p>
<p>To enable the benefits of new AI technologies for better chip design flows and methodologies, TSMC has been working with its partners to create new AI-driven flows, and supporting them with AI Design Kits (ADK).</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24282066" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/tsmc7.png?resize=1248%2C704&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="1248" height="704" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/tsmc7.png?w=1248&amp;ssl=1 1248w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/tsmc7.png?resize=300%2C169&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/tsmc7.png?resize=1024%2C578&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/tsmc7.png?resize=768%2C433&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/tsmc7.png?resize=600%2C338&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><br />
<strong>Fig. 7: TSMC AI design kit for agentic AI. Source: TSMC</strong></p>
<p>Figure 7 shows the new proposed framework for AI-driven design enabled by TSMC’s ADKs. The close industry collaboration is supporting the tremendous growth in AI by using AI. The forecasts for the next four years continue to show immense growth in these markets, as well as the technologies needed to enable that growth.</p>

		<title>Why Verification Needs a Thread, Not More Fragments</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/why-verification-needs-a-thread-not-more-fragments/</link>
					<comments>https://semiengineering.com/why-verification-needs-a-thread-not-more-fragments/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Jake Wiltgen]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Tue, 29 Sep 2026 07:01:46 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Best Of Both: LP & HP]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Blogs - LPHP]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Low Power-High Performance]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Siemens EDA]]></category>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Why traceability at scale is so critical.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/why-verification-needs-a-thread-not-more-fragments/">Why Verification Needs a Thread, Not More Fragments</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p><strong>By Jake Wiltgen and Mike Andrews</strong></p>
<p>As systems become more software-defined, safety-aware, and integration-heavy, verification is pushed into a role it was never meant to play. In many organizations, it is treated as a downstream activity: a collection of tests, regressions, dashboards, coverage reports, and signoff reviews that happen after design decisions are already in motion.</p>
<p>That model is increasingly out of step with reality. Modern products are not verified in one place, by one team, against one stable specification. They are assembled across hardware, software, subsystem, and system domains. Meanwhile, requirements evolve, configurations shift, and IP is reused in new contexts. Safety, security, and quality objectives overlap. And the evidence needed to explain whether something is verified can be scattered across tools, teams, and handoffs.</p>
<p>This is the growing verification challenge: not simply running more tests but maintaining meaning across the lifecycle.</p>
<p>For years, the industry has responded to complexity by adding more verification engines, more automation, and more data. Those are all necessary. But they do not, by themselves, solve the underlying problem. More activity does not automatically create more understanding. In fact, without a way to connect intent, execution, and outcome, it often creates the opposite: a larger pile of disconnected proof points that are difficult to interpret, trust, or reuse.</p>
<p>That is why verification is beginning to shift from a tool-centric exercise to a thread-centric discipline.</p>
<p><strong>The real bottleneck is traceability at scale</strong><br />
Traceability is often discussed as if it were mainly a compliance issue: something needed for audits, safety certification, or customer documentation. That view is too narrow. In advanced electronic systems, traceability is becoming an operational requirement for engineering itself.</p>
<p>When a requirement changes, teams need to know what verification intent is affected, what tests are relevant, what environments were used, what assumptions were embedded, and whether previous results still apply. When a subsystem is reused, they need to understand not just that it passed verification once, but under what conditions and against which parameters. When issues emerge late in the cycle, they need to determine whether the problem is a design defect, an environment mismatch, a requirements gap, or a breakdown in verification continuity.</p>
<p>Without that level of traceability, verification becomes expensive in a specific way. Engineers are forced to reconstruct context manually. Results must be rediscovered rather than reused. Reviews become debates over interpretation instead of decisions based on evidence. And signoff becomes less about confidence and more about whether the organization can live with ambiguity.</p>
<p>This is manageable in smaller projects. It becomes dangerous in complex ones.</p>
<p>The challenge is compounded by the fact that today’s systems are not bound neatly within a single abstraction layer. A requirement may originate at the system level, then be refined in software, implemented in hardware, constrained by safety goals, and validated through multiple verification technologies. If each domain captures evidence independently, then the organization may have plenty of data and still lack a coherent answer to a simple question: what exactly do we know, and why do we believe it?</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24281582" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/siemens1.png?resize=624%2C276&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="624" height="276" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/siemens1.png?w=624&amp;ssl=1 624w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/siemens1.png?resize=300%2C133&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/siemens1.png?resize=600%2C265&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 624px) 100vw, 624px" /><br />
<strong>Fig. 1:  A sampling of questions that a comprehensive verification thread answers.</strong></p>
<p>That is where verification threading matters.</p>
<p><strong>Verification data is not enough without verification context</strong><br />
Most verification environments are good at producing outputs. They generate logs, waveforms, assertions, coverage metrics, pass/fail status, fault campaign results, and test artifacts. The problem is that these outputs are often stored as local evidence rather than lifecycle knowledge.</p>
<p>A passing regression result, for example, has limited value if it is disconnected from the requirement it was intended to address, the configuration under which it ran, the version of the design and testbench involved, and the assumptions that governed the scenario. The same is true for a coverage number. Coverage can indicate progress, but without context it cannot explain sufficiency. It says something happened, not necessarily why it matters.</p>
<p>That distinction becomes critical as verification scales. What organizations need is not just evidence that verification occurred, but a durable way to connect that evidence to engineering intent.</p>
<p>This is the essence of a verification thread: a structured digital linkage between requirements, parameters, verification activities, configurations, and results across the lifecycle. Instead of treating verification as a series of isolated local events, it treats each event as part of a larger body of knowledge.</p>
<p>That sounds abstract until you consider the alternative, which is what many teams live with today: a fragmented verification model where requirements live in one system, tests in another, results in another, reviews in slide decks, and engineering rationale in people’s heads. That may work while the original team is intact and the schedule is forgiving. But it doesn’t work as well when projects are reused, audited, scaled, or handed across organizational boundaries.</p>
<p><strong>From reporting artifacts to reusable engineering evidence</strong><br />
One of the more important shifts in this model is conceptual. Verification artifacts should no longer be seen merely as reports of completed work. They should be treated as reusable evidence objects.</p>
<p>That means each meaningful verification event needs to capture more than a binary result. It needs to preserve the context that makes the result interpretable. What requirement or intent did this activity address? What parameters defined the expected behavior? What design version, environment, stimulus, and constraints were involved? What dependencies or linked evidence help explain the outcome?</p>
<p>When captured in a structured way, this creates a much richer verification fabric. A result is no longer just a line in a regression summary; it is part of a queryable network of engineering evidence. This has several implications.</p>
<p>First, verification becomes more explainable. Teams can move beyond “we ran the test” to “we can show how this requirement was verified, under which conditions, with which evidence, and what remains open.”</p>
<p>Second, verification becomes more reusable. Prior work is assessed for applicability instead of repeated blindly or discarded reflexively. This is especially valuable in derivative designs, platform-based development, and subsystem reuse.</p>
<p>Third, verification becomes more resilient to change. When requirements, configurations, or architectures evolve, impacts can be traced through linked evidence rather than rediscovered by brute force.</p>
<p>And fourth, verification becomes more measurable at the program level. Management is no longer limited to activity metrics such as number of tests run or regressions completed. It can evaluate actual verification readiness, evidence completeness, and requirement-level closure.</p>
<p>That is a much more useful basis for decision-making.</p>
<p><strong>Why this matters now</strong><br />
The need for a digital verification thread is not new, but the urgency is. Three industry shifts are colliding.</p>
<p>The first is system complexity. Heterogeneous integration, software-defined functionality, AI-enabled behavior, and safety/security requirements have all increased the number of relationships that matter during verification. The hard part is no longer only validating blocks. It is maintaining consistency and explainability across interactions.</p>
<p>The second is organizational distribution. Verification is now performed across teams, geographies, suppliers, and lifecycle stages. The tacit knowledge that used to hold flows together does not scale well in distributed development. If context is not captured explicitly, it is lost.</p>
<p>The third is the rising cost of late ambiguity. As tapeouts become more expensive and product schedules more compressed, organizations have less tolerance for uncertainty at signoff. They need stronger answers earlier: not only whether something passed, but whether the evidence is complete, connected, and defensible.</p>
<p>This is why verification threading should be viewed as an engineering infrastructure issue, not a documentation enhancement. It is about building continuity into the verification process itself.</p>
<p><strong>A thread has to span domains, not just tools</strong><br />
One trap in discussions about digital threads is assuming the problem is simply one of tool integration. Tool interoperability matters, of course. But a true verification thread requires something deeper than moving data between applications.</p>
<p>It requires a normalized way to represent verification intent and evidence across domains.</p>
<p>That matters because hardware verification, software validation, system testing, safety analysis, and requirements management all describe the world differently. They use different abstractions, different objects, and different success criteria. If the only connection between them is file exchange, then the thread remains fragile.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24281583" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/siemens2.png?resize=498%2C356&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="498" height="356" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/siemens2.png?w=498&amp;ssl=1 498w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/siemens2.png?resize=300%2C214&amp;ssl=1 300w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 498px) 100vw, 498px" /><br />
<strong>Fig. 2: Multi-domain verification threading.</strong></p>
<p>A stronger model is to connect them through shared semantics, requirements, parameters, configurations, and evidence objects that can be related even when they originate in different environments. In practice, this creates a kind of engineering knowledge graph, where verification results are not merely stored but linked in ways that preserve meaning.</p>
<p>This is what enables cross-domain reasoning. A team can trace from a system requirement to the verification activities that support it. It can understand which parameterized conditions were exercised. It can identify where evidence is missing, duplicated, stale, or no longer valid after a change. And it can do this without manually stitching together spreadsheets and slide decks at every review.</p>
<p>That is a vastly different operating model from conventional traceability, which too often becomes a static matrix maintained for process reasons, rather than as an active engineering asset.</p>
<p><strong>The discipline behind the thread</strong><br />
Of course, none of this works if the underlying verification intent is vague.</p>
<p>A digital verification thread is only as useful as the quality of the information captured within it. That means requirements must be decomposed into verifiable expectations. Parameters must be explicit rather than implied. Verification events must be recorded in a structured way — not as free-form commentary after the fact.</p>
<p>This is where many teams discover that the problem is not just tooling, but discipline. If requirements are ambiguous, then traceability becomes performative. If parameters are not defined, then reuse becomes risky. If verification evidence is captured inconsistently, then the thread becomes patchy and unreliable.</p>
<p>But that is also why the payoff is significant. The discipline required to build a verification thread improves engineering quality even before the full benefits of lifecycle traceability are realized. It forces teams to clarify intent, define expected behavior more precisely, and connect verification work to actual design objectives. In other words, the thread is not just a record of verification maturity. It helps create it.</p>
<p><strong>Verification threading changes the value of signoff</strong><br />
Traditionally, signoff has been treated as the moment when enough verification has accumulated to justify moving forward. In a fragmented environment, that often means assembling evidence from many places and asking experienced people to decide whether the overall picture feels acceptable.</p>
<p>That process is not going away entirely. Engineering judgment will always matter. But verification threading changes what signoff can be.</p>
<p>Instead of being a high-pressure reconciliation exercise, signoff can become the natural outcome of a continuously connected verification model. Evidence is linked to intent. Changes have been propagated through the thread. Gaps are visible earlier. Reuse claims are more defensible. Reviews focus less on gathering proof and more on interpreting risk.</p>
<p>That shift matters for productivity, but it matters even more for confidence.</p>
<p>Ultimately the issue is not whether organizations can produce verification artifacts. Most can. The issue is whether they can explain verification completeness in a way that scales with system complexity. As products become more integrated and more adaptive, that ability will separate teams that are merely busy from teams that are in control.</p>
<p><strong>The next step is to make verification knowledge durable</strong></p>
<p>The semiconductor industry has invested heavily in generating verification data. The next frontier is making that data durable, connected, and reusable as engineering knowledge.</p>
<p>That is the promise of verification threading. It turns verification from an opaque collection of local activities into a lifecycle asset, one that supports reuse, accelerates impact analysis, improves explainability, and strengthens signoff confidence across hardware, software, and systems.</p>
<p>For organizations wrestling with fragmented traceability, the answer is not another dashboard. It is a better verification thread.</p>
<p>For a deeper look at how your team can build a digital verification thread, I suggest reading the white paper “<a href="https://verificationacademy.com/topics/coverage/questa-one-verithreader-rethinking-verification-traceability-for-modern-systems/">Rethinking Traceability for Modern Systems</a>” which discusses how Questa One VeriThreader helps solve this emerging challenge.</p>
<p><strong>— Mike Andrews is a technical product manager at Siemens EDA, responsible for the VeriThreader coverage and verification threading solution.</strong></p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/why-verification-needs-a-thread-not-more-fragments/">Why Verification Needs a Thread, Not More Fragments</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>

		<item>
		<title>Moores Lab AI: Applying Agentic AI Across Chip Design</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/moores-law-ai-applying-agentic-ai-across-chip-design/</link>
					<comments>https://semiengineering.com/moores-law-ai-applying-agentic-ai-across-chip-design/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Brendan Heffernan]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Tue, 29 Sep 2026 07:01:00 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Startup Corner]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[System-Level Design]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[agentic AI]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[AI]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[EDA startup]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Moores Lab AI]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://semiengineering.com/?p=24282014</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>EDA startup bets on domain expertise to speed the design process.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/moores-law-ai-applying-agentic-ai-across-chip-design/">Moores Lab AI: Applying Agentic AI Across Chip Design</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>With the AI boom driving demand for faster semiconductor chip turnarounds, <a href="https://semiengineering.com/ai-in-chip-design-lots-of-promise-plenty-of-unanswered-questions/">can AI help engineers meet those tighter deadlines</a>?</p>
<p>Startup Moores Lab AI hopes to provide a definitive answer with its end-to-end chip design automation products. Founded last year by chip industry veterans, the company contends that for AI agents to solve chip design problems, they must be designed by people with deep chip design expertise.</p>
<p>“Most of the startups in the same space trying to automate semiconductor flows are all coming from the AI background,&#8221; said Shelly Henry, the company&#8217;s CEO and co-founder. &#8220;We come from the other side. We are semiconductor engineers. We found a new technology in AI and thought about how we can use it to solve our problems. There are two schools of thought there. Their approach is, ‘Let&#8217;s make this AI better and better so that it will automatically solve semiconductor problems.’ We are saying, ‘AI is already getting better; let&#8217;s build something on top of it.’ That&#8217;s where our differentiation is.”</p>
<p>Moores Lab AI&#8217;s initial focus is on speeding up verification, debugging, and coverage. “It comes with its own challenges, but what we have built is a technology using AI that will enable you to actually build chips in under six months, from start to finish,” Henry said. “When you&#8217;re building a chip, you&#8217;re betting on a market two years down the line. It takes a lot of money and effort for those two years to build that chip. We have been trying as a community to reduce this cycle so that it becomes more predictable and less expensive, so that more startups and new endeavors can come into this field.”</p>
<p>The company is also developing a suite of products to automate complex SoC development and verification.</p>
<p>So far, the biggest productivity gains the company’s products have delivered have come through speeding the initial debug phase, Henry said. “We have our system deployed in about 10 different places, and they are using it for different kinds of IP. They&#8217;re seeing the biggest jump in initial setup. Usually, it takes about three to four months to get your test plan ready, your test bench ready, and to get all your simulations running, or even the first simulation to run and find the first bug. We consistently see customers jump to the first bug within 48 hours using our platform. All our customers are saying the same thing. That initial thing is compressed right off the bat. Then once they find the first bug, they continuously use our platform to find more and more bugs very quickly.”</p>
<p>But developing these tools has revealed some of the inherent challenges in trusting agentic AI to deliver 100% reliable chips.</p>
<p>“If you throw a spec at any kind of LLM or any kind of AI agent, it is bound to miss 20% to 30% of the intricacies of the spec,” Henry said. “It&#8217;s a very specific challenge within our industry, because building semiconductors is a zero-tolerance industry. If you have a bug, it&#8217;s a $10M problem because you can&#8217;t patch it or work around it. You have to rebuild the whole fleet of chips again. That&#8217;s why we spend so much time and effort on verification. That is the process we are trying to address and make really fast.”</p>
<p>That non-existent margin of error is also what makes the cross-disciplinary chip design expertise on Moores Lab AI’s staff so essential.</p>
<p>“It&#8217;s a very complex process and involves about 200 engineers. All these engineers have different specialties — design engineers, architects, verification engineers, DFT engineers, physical layout engineers, synthesis engineers,” he said. “We have to break down that problem into all these specialties and how we can build an AI system to accelerate these different specialties so that the final thing will compress. That has been our holy grail — how to get all these things working with AI.”</p>
<p>Henry said that one of the biggest challenges for his company going forward will be demonstrating results to engineering teams in a way that clearly cuts through the AI hype.</p>
<p>“It&#8217;s a challenging time for our customers, because there is a lot of noise in this space and they&#8217;re getting bombarded with all these offers,” Henry said. “Our new approach is to say, ‘Let us come in, take up one project, and show you what we can deliver. At the end of that project, it will match and exceed what your engineers have done for that exact project over the last nine years. Once we demonstrate that, then let&#8217;s talk about the next project.’ That&#8217;s been very well received.”</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/moores-law-ai-applying-agentic-ai-across-chip-design/">Moores Lab AI: Applying Agentic AI Across Chip Design</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></content:encoded>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Researchers at <strong>Purdue University</strong> and the <strong>UCLA</strong> published a technical paper titled “Experimental Evidence for the Impact of Copper Microstructure on Residual Stress of Through Silicon Via.”</p>
<p class="wp-block-paragraph"><strong>Abstract Excerpt:</strong></p>
<p>“Here, we experimentally quantify the impact of Cu microstructure on the TSV-induced residual stress within silicon. A 3-⁢m-diameter TSV array was annealed at 400 °C for 60 min, and the residual stress in the surrounding Si was imaged with Raman spectroscopy at room temperature. The Cu surface microstructure was characterized with electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) to deduce the microstructure dependent effective elastic modulus.&#8221;</p>
<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Find the <a href="https://advanced.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/aelm.70600">technical paper here</a>. September 2026.</p>
<p class="wp-block-paragraph">S. Lyu, T. Beechem, and T. Wei, “ Experimental Evidence for the Impact of Copper Microstructure on Residual Stress of Through Silicon Via.” Advanced Electronic Materials (2026): e70600. https://doi.org/10.1002/aelm.70600  </p>

		<item>
		<title>Intuition and AI</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/intuition-and-ai/</link>
					<comments>https://semiengineering.com/intuition-and-ai/#comments</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Brian Bailey]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Mon, 28 Sep 2026 07:01:56 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Opinion]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[System-Level Design]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[What Were They Thinking]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[AI]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[creative thinking]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[intuition]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://semiengineering.com/?p=24281998</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Can AI be creative? It is impossible to know unless we understand what creativity really means, and that's difficult to describe.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/intuition-and-ai/">Intuition and AI</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>From Wikipedia: &#8220;Intuition is the ability to acquire knowledge without recourse to conscious reasoning or needing an explanation. Different fields use the word &#8220;intuition&#8221; in very different ways, including but not limited to: direct access to unconscious knowledge; unconscious cognition; gut feelings; inner sensing; inner insight to unconscious pattern-recognition; and the ability to understand something instinctively, without any need for conscious reasoning.&#8221;</p>
<p>Is AI capable of intuition, and is that what is necessary for creativity? While I am no expert in the latest developments in AI, I am surprised this has not created more discussion amongst the AI companies. To me, this question is perhaps one of the most important when it comes to the notion of the singularity. Can AI truly innovate, or can it only develop optimizations based on information it has gathered from the past?</p>
<p>That last part of the statement is troubling because the past is unreliable. It is biased and far from being complete. Moreover, history is written from the perspective of the winners in a battle, or by those who have the money, power, or control to ensure the narrative of the past says what they want others to see. We have only to see the power of the pen in the current U.S. administration. It is enough to attempt to change history, to suppress aspects of it, to rename things that are accepted names internationally, and to hide data that does not fit with their policies. The past, and indeed the present, are unreliable sources.</p>
<p>AI will never forget recent history. You can suppress data, but once it has been published and seen by AI, it will never be forgotten. It was hard enough to make the previous generation of software delete information on demand. AI now creates synthetic information based on actual information, such that it no longer knows its source, or the variants created, and therefore can never identify where something came from when told to delete it.</p>
<p>But does intuition or innovation depend on information from the past? Knowledge can constrain a problem by providing evidence about things that do not work, or that are not possible because of physics. Within senior engineers, myself included, that can also be considered a detriment. Just because we tried something in the past and it proved to be not possible, or not the best option, does not mean it is impossible today. The same experiment run 30 years apart may indeed lead to different results because the underlying assumptions or limitations have changed. I am sure that, given a clean sheet of paper with no restrictions based on legacy, many of the things we do today would be different, such as the processor/memory relationship.</p>
<p>Some of the greatest psychologists have disagreed about intuition for over a hundred years. Freud thinks that intuition is basically not possible, that all knowledge has to come from intellectual manipulation of known observations. Jung, on the other hand, sees intuition as an irrational function linked to &#8220;perception via the unconscious.&#8221; To add a third hand, Klein suggests that intuition is a pattern-matching process under a time constraint, leading to analysis as a deliberate review to assess feasibility.</p>
<p>I would like to add some personal examples, not in an attempt to make myself seem special, but to act as a place to argue from. I have been described as an intuitive person. In one example, two of the senior members of the development team were discussing how to solve a particular problem. It was a timing problem that included reconvergent fanout. It was a Friday afternoon, and we had been out at the pub having a few pints, as was normal. They were stuck and getting frustrated. I suddenly blurted out, &#8216;Why don&#8217;t you maintain the equations symbolically and solve when necessary.&#8217; There was stunned silence. Then one of them said, &#8216;That is brilliant,&#8217; and they spent the next 18 months implementing it. I did not know about symbolic solvers, only that it seemed a logical way of tackling the problem. Was that intuitive, or was I just lucky? Everyone gets it right every now and then.</p>
<p>Another behavior I have been guilty of is subconscious explanation. On several occasions, I have said something that has been judged to be of value. When asked to repeat, I basically cannot do it, barely even remembering the important points of what I just said. What I said never reached my conscious mind.</p>
<p>A last example was in college. This was back in the &#8217;70s, and a final-year course was on microprocessor design. At the beginning of the first lecture, the lecturer said this was very different from everything we had already studied, and that many of the class would have problems with it. We had just come back from our final sabbatical period, and I was confused by his statement and the course outline. At the end of the lecture, I talked to him about what I had been working on during the sabbatical and what I planned for my dissertation. He was stunned and told me that I need not take the class because I was already way beyond anything he was going to teach us. I had only read data sheets about commercially available parts and then just got on with it. It all seemed quite obvious to me.</p>
<p>Was microprocessor design obvious to someone who was not stuck in a historical way of thinking? Is this just an example of how senior engineers view new grads today — ones that are AI native and can see past problems in a way that historical thinking shuts out? Have I ever actually been creative in the sense of creating something new that wasn&#8217;t directly based on my experiences? I honestly don’t know.</p>
<p>I have been told I am creative and intuitive. But I don&#8217;t see why AI couldn&#8217;t have done the same as me, and maybe much more. My only claim is that I probably did it faster, using less energy. Give me a pint and you may get some wisdom in return.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/intuition-and-ai/">Intuition and AI</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></content:encoded>

		<title>One Substrate No Longer Rules Them All</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/one-substrate-no-longer-rules-them-all/</link>
					<comments>https://semiengineering.com/one-substrate-no-longer-rules-them-all/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Gregory Haley]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Mon, 28 Sep 2026 07:01:09 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Manufacturing, Packaging and Materials]]></category>

		<category><![CDATA[glass substrates]]></category>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Larger packages, finer routing, and embedded functions are pushing advanced substrates toward application-specific designs.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/one-substrate-no-longer-rules-them-all/">One Substrate No Longer Rules Them All</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p><strong>Key Takeaways</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>Larger body sizes, higher layer counts, finer routing, and embedded functions are increasingly making substrate capability application-specific.</li>
<li>A substrate can be technically feasible but impractical at the yield or process window required for high-volume manufacturing.</li>
<li>As substrates specialize, the carrier systems, temporary bonding materials, and many process flows around them must specialize, as well.</li>
</ul>
<hr />
<p>For years, the substrate problem was relatively easy to describe, even when it was difficult to solve. Make enough of them, at the required dimensions and yield, and advanced packaging lines can keep moving.</p>
<p>The shortages that put ABF substrates on executive dashboards reinforced that view, and capacity remains a big part of the overall equation. But a supplier can have available capacity and still be unable to build the substrate needed for a modern advanced package. Larger bodies, more layers, finer routing, new dielectrics, embedded components, and tighter mechanical tolerances often arrive together, turning a supply problem into a capability problem.</p>
<p>Economics are beginning to expose the shift. More money is being spent on substrates without a proportional increase in the number of substrates shipped, because each one requires more material and more structure. In AI and server packages, that generally means larger areas, additional layers, and more demanding interconnect requirements.</p>
<p>“Substrate value is rising faster than shipment volume because packages are using higher layer counts and larger body sizes, which increase material consumption,” said Yu-Po Wang, principal consultant at Prismark<strong>,</strong> in a recent conference presentation. “The strongest growth area is still servers, particularly large-body flip-chip BGA packages.”</p>
<p><strong>Capacity for what?</strong><br />
The old capacity question now has a qualifier attached to it — capacity for what? Even if two suppliers make organic substrates for roughly the same package footprint, they might not be interchangeable. Each package architecture imposes its own acceptable combination of materials, dimensions, and process limits, so matching the footprint is just the beginning. Dielectric properties, line and space, layer stack, CTE, embedded passives, power delivery, thermal behavior, and the assembly flow can significantly narrow material choices. That narrowing begins with the growing amount of system functionality being pushed into the package itself.</p>
<p>Chiplets help address part of the silicon-scaling problem by allowing large systems to be divided into smaller dies and combined later. But the functions that once lived together on a single piece of silicon still need to communicate after they’re separated. Signals have to cross the package, power has to reach each die without excessive loss or noise, and HBM has to sit close enough to logic to realize bandwidth benefits.</p>
<p>“From the package point of view, the package is not just a protector. It’s actually carrying quite a bit of signal and power,” said Tarek Ibrahim, senior principal engineer at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/intel-foundry/">Intel Foundry</a>, in a recent presentation. “So we optimize the dielectric and the design rule working with our vendors, equipment suppliers, as well as our substrate suppliers.”</p>
<p>Those additions turn what used to look like packaging choices into system decisions. A dielectric is selected based on the influence of its electrical properties on signal propagation, not because it survives lamination and assembly. Layer count affects routing capacity and power delivery. Embedded passives can shorten electrical paths but consume area and add process steps, while optical integration brings its own geometries, materials, and thermal sensitivities. The substrate is still underneath the dies, but it is increasingly doing work that determines how well the dies function together.</p>
<p>The specialization happens within substrate families, as well as between them. Organic substrates are no longer broadly interchangeable when different packages require different core structures, layer counts, and embedded functions.</p>
<p>“We have three types of core-layer structures and four-, six- and eight-layer cores,” said Yasushi Araki, corporate officer and general manager of R&amp;D at Shinko Electric<strong>,</strong> in a recent conference presentation. “Now customers are asking us to embed passive components in the core for power integrity.”</p>
<p>This makes the familiar organic-versus-silicon-versus-glass debate somewhat misleading. Those remain important architectural choices, but specialization is already occurring inside each category. That specialization becomes more consequential when the design has to be manufactured repeatedly rather than demonstrated once. A layout tool can draw a finer line, and a package architect can ask for another build-up layer, but neither decision proves that a supplier can make millions of those substrates at an acceptable yield.</p>
<p><strong>Yield makes the real design rules</strong><br />
The boundary between what can be designed and what can be manufactured shows up when customer architecture, OSAT assembly rules and substrate supplier process limits have to coexist. With new advanced packaging dimensions, the design rule has to survive more than one manufacturing window. A geometry that works for the package architecture still has to be something the substrate supplier can yield and the OSAT can assemble reliably.</p>
<p>“We may want certain design rules, but the substrate supplier may tell us that if we do that, it will hit their yield because these are large-body, multilayer structures,” said Joe Roybal, senior vice president and general manager of the Mainstream Business Unit at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/amkor-technology/">Amkor</a>. “We need to make sure the yield is reasonable, and at some point we also have to adapt our assembly process, whether that is standard mass reflow, laser-assisted bonding or thermocompression bonding.”</p>
<p>A specification therefore can remain technically achievable while becoming economically unattractive. More layers introduce more chances for defects and registration errors. Larger body sizes give dimensional and mechanical variation more distance over which to accumulate, while tighter routing reduces process margin. The difficulty is rarely one spectacular failure mechanism, though. More often, it is the narrowing of several tolerances at once until a substrate supplier’s nominal capability no longer translates cleanly into production yield. The loss of repeatability across designs may be just as important.</p>
<p>“These days, we don’t get to say, ‘Oh, we’ve done this one before,’” added Roybal. “Each customer is different, and there is development work we need to do before we’re ready for verification and high-volume manufacturing.”</p>
<p>Body size, die placement, pitch, and thermal constraints can differ enough that an established process window becomes a starting point rather than a reusable answer. That changes what “second source” means, as well.</p>
<p>A supplier with unused factory capacity still must reproduce the required stack, dimensions, electrical behavior, and process yield before it becomes an interchangeable source. As the substrate becomes more specific to the architecture, the qualified supply base can become much smaller than the nominal supply base, and that specialization begins to propagate into materials that are not part of the finished substrate at all.</p>
<p><strong>The stack changes the material</strong><br />
A substrate does not travel through assembly untouched. Depending on the flow, it may be attached temporarily to a carrier, heated and cooled repeatedly, coated with dielectric, exposed to plasma or wet chemistry, plated, thinned, debonded, and cleaned. Each operation renders the next one a physical structure with a history, including residual stress, warpage, surface condition, and materials that have already seen several chemical and temperature excursions.</p>
<p>Temporary bonding materials sit in the middle of that history. They may come into contact with polymers, dielectrics, metals, silicon or glass, and they need to hold increasingly thin structures securely through processing without becoming so stiff that they introduce additional mechanical stress. Those requirements can change with the surfaces involved, the thermal budget, and the amount of warpage the material has to accommodate.</p>
<p>“The design of these materials should be very application specific,” said Hamed Derami, advanced semiconductor packaging materials manager at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/brewer-science/">Brewer Science</a>. “One temporary bond material might work for a specific process and not another. We usually redesign the material around what it will come into contact with and the adhesion requirements of that process.”</p>
<p>That process window can be narrow. Too little adhesion and the package can delaminate during processing. Too high a modulus and the temporary-bond layer can add stress instead of buffering it. Total thickness variation also matters when fine-pitch RDL is built over the bonded structure, because local thickness variation can degrade RDL uniformity and resolution across the wafer. As a result, Brewer tunes the material around adhesion, thermal budget, warpage, and the other requirements of a particular process flow, rather than assuming one chemistry will work across different architectures.</p>
<p>That change doesn&#8217;t always require a new package architecture. A different mold compound can alter adhesion and mechanical loading, while changes in cure conditions or thermal budget can affect polymer behavior. “Even if they go from version one of their packaging to version two, we might need to change our material,” added Derami.</p>
<p>Moving from wafer to panel adds another set of demands. Non-uniform coatings, along with higher stress and warpage, can require temporary-bond materials with greater thermal and mechanical stability for panel-level packaging.</p>
<p>Glass shows the same dependency inside the permanent substrate. A copper-filled through-glass via expands and contracts differently from the surrounding glass as the structure heats and cools because the materials have different CTEs. Applied Materials found that lowering the CTE of the liner between them was not sufficient by itself. If the liner modulus remained too high, it could not deform enough to absorb the strain, while a low-CTE, low-modulus liner reduced cracking by addressing both the thermal mismatch and the mechanical response.</p>
<p>“There are a lot of questions around the idea that changing the glass material changes the process,” said Poulomi Mukherjee, process integration engineer for advanced packaging at Applied Materials, in a recent conference presentation. “That led us to understand that we need to have a solution that works for different types of glass so that the downstream processes don’t change.”</p>
<p>The objective is process portability, but the need to engineer that portability exposes the underlying problem. “Glass” is not one set of mechanical and interfacial conditions. Change the composition or properties enough and stress, seed adhesion, and downstream thermal behavior can change with it.</p>
<p>“All these process steps have their own challenges,” Mukherjee said. “They have to work individually, as well as work in a co-optimized way together, so that the upstream and downstream processes do not interfere with each other.”</p>
<p>By this point, substrate specialization has escaped the substrate factory. The carrier can change, the adhesive can change, the liner can change, and the acceptable process window can change. The next constraint lands on the equipment expected to process all of those variations.</p>
<p><strong>Equipment must evolve</strong><br />
After substrate choices alter materials, stress, handling, and process sequence, equipment makers inherit the variation. A tool that was designed around a familiar wafer thickness, dielectric system, or via process may have to operate across larger panels, more build-up layers, and tighter line-and-space requirements — all while maintaining uniformity over a much larger area. That creates its own development problem for equipment suppliers as larger substrates, tighter routing requirements, and multiple emerging process options push tools beyond familiar process windows.</p>
<p>“The industry has not yet converged on what the real paradigm will be, and all of these approaches require a lot more investment and development from the equipment industry,” said Prahalad Parthangal, technical director of advanced packaging at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/lam-research/">Lam Research</a>, in a recent conference presentation. “We need to understand how we standardize and how we develop something that is fully capable of sustaining the industry.”</p>
<p>Until that convergence happens, equipment suppliers may have to support several competing substrate approaches without knowing which one(s) ultimately will reach high-volume manufacturing.</p>
<p>This creates an awkward capital-equipment problem. The equipment has to be developed early enough to enable a substrate technology, but the technology may still be competing with several alternatives. A glass-core flow may need different handling and via processing than an organic build-up substrate. Panel processing introduces its own deposition and uniformity requirements, while finer routing can push back-end processes toward techniques that look increasingly like front-end manufacturing. Supporting specialization therefore means designing and purchasing equipment before the eventual production mix is fully known.</p>
<p>That uncertainty is easier to justify when one application dominates the roadmap. However, the substrate market is heading in the opposite direction with AI, optics, automotive, and power packages pulling design requirements toward different endpoints.</p>
<p><strong>The best choice depends on what the package has to do</strong><br />
AI and HPC are currently pushing some of the most aggressive substrate requirements. Large logic complexes surrounded by HBM need dense routing, many layers, high-speed signaling, and increasingly difficult power delivery, while the package itself grows in both area and value. Those requirements favor technologies that can support large body sizes and high wiring density, but they do not establish a universal architecture for everything else.</p>
<p>Co-packaged optics is already exposing how quickly the hierarchy can change. The electronics, photonic ICs, optical engines, fiber attachment, and thermal solution have to coexist inside one package, and the manufacturing infrastructure is still developing around several competing implementations.</p>
<p>“One of the challenges here is because it’s so new and everybody is kind of trying to blaze their own trail,” said Suresh Jayaraman, senior director of package development at Amkor. “Each solution is kind of unique, and everybody’s building custom solutions. If we invest and say, okay, we’re going to support this particular architecture, it may or may not port over to someone else.”</p>
<p>The differences reach directly into assembly. Some CPO approaches can reuse elements of an existing 2.5D platform, but optical components do not behave like ordinary dies. Attaching them can require equipment that was not previously part of the OSAT toolbox, while small amounts of contamination that might be tolerable in an electronic package can attenuate light around micro-lens arrays. Manufacturers consequently have to consider new attachment, cleaning, and inspection capabilities for those optical structures.</p>
<p>Even the material immediately around the optical path can vary by architecture. Some architectures use an index-matching epoxy to attach the lens to the interposer, while others require a clean air cavity instead. A substrate or interposer optimized for conventional electronic routing may remain useful as a starting platform, but the optical architecture can force enough changes around it that the manufacturing flow becomes application-specific.</p>
<p>Automotive demonstrates the opposite pressure. It is adopting more advanced packaging for ADAS and centralized compute, but much of the market continues to rely on mature package types because qualification history, cost, and long-term reliability carry different weight than they do in a leading-edge AI accelerator.</p>
<p>“Although we’re seeing significant growth in advanced packages, the workhorse of automotive packaging still remains traditional wire-bond packages,” said Prasad Dhond, vice president of BGA and QFN products at Amkor. “We’re using material sets driven by lower cost and higher reliability, along with automotive-specific design features such as wettable flanks that improve inspectability.”</p>
<p>That contrast is important because specialization doesn’t always mean moving to the most advanced substrate available. An AI processor might accept additional layers, expensive materials, and aggressive integration to gain bandwidth. Many automotive applications still favor mature architectures with long reliability histories. High-voltage power devices emphasize thermal paths, isolation, and materials capable of surviving very different electrical stresses, while CPO adds optical cleanliness and alignment constraints. The substrate hierarchy changes because the optimization target changes.</p>
<p><strong>More suppliers do not necessarily mean more supply</strong><br />
The divergence has a supply-chain consequence that can be easy to miss when capacity is discussed in aggregate. A substrate supplier may have open production capacity, but qualification depends on whether it can reproduce a particular layer stack, material system, dimensions, and the yield needed for the design. As those combinations become more specialized, switching suppliers becomes less like buying an equivalent part and more like qualifying another manufacturing process.</p>
<p>The stakes rise quickly when the substrate sits beneath expensive logic and memory. Intel Foundry is working with partners to bring more silicon-like yield infrastructure into substrate manufacturing as package size and the amount of embedded silicon increase.</p>
<p>“At the end of the day, I’m trying to maintain a known good substrate, so when I attach the silicon, I’m avoiding any loss due to the substrate being not functional,” said Intel’s Ibrahim.</p>
<p>That changes the economics of substrate quality. A defect in a relatively inexpensive substrate is one problem before assembly, and a much more expensive problem after high-value logic and HBM have been attached. As package cost rises, inspection, process control, and substrate qualification have to move upstream because the package can no longer afford to discover substrate failure at the end.</p>
<p>The same logic makes second sourcing more difficult. A nominally compatible supplier has to demonstrate that it can meet the specifications, and do so repeatedly enough to protect everything subsequently assembled on top of it. Capacity remains important, but useful capacity is the portion that has been qualified for that particular architecture.</p>
<p><strong>Design files have to become more specific, too</strong><br />
Physical specialization creates a less visible problem upstream. Engineers can’t optimize a substrate as part of the electrical, thermal, and mechanical system if the design environment knows only its outline, routing rules and a few nominal material properties. That becomes particularly difficult when the substrate, RDL, interposer and assembly process come from different suppliers.</p>
<p>“There is still a lot of opaqueness around standardized information for package substrates, RDLs and interposers,” said Amlendu Shekhar Choubey, senior director of product management for the 3DIC Compiler platform at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/synopsys-inc/">Synopsys</a>. “Material technology files for thermal and power behavior for interposers and substrates, in a format that can be integrated into the design flow, are still lacking.”</p>
<p>Thermal behavior belongs to the complete stack, not any one component. The die, mold, interposer, substrate, and even the PCB beneath the package influence the result. Leaving those pieces out can make the thermal analysis wrong. As substrate architectures become more specialized, their digital descriptions need to capture more of that electrical, thermal, and mechanical behavior, as well.</p>
<p>That is difficult in an ecosystem built around proprietary processes. Suppliers need to expose enough information for system-level analysis without revealing the manufacturing details that differentiate them. Bhatt described materials suppliers, equipment makers, and fabs as separate “black boxes” that increasingly need to exchange enough information to iterate together.</p>
<p>“There isn’t going to be one solution that fits all. Every process is going to require some customization,” said Sanjiv Bhatt, senior director of marketing and business development at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/mitsubishi-chemical-group/">Mitsubishi Chemical Group</a>. “For that customization, one person cannot do it all. You have to have collaboration that allows you to move forward.”</p>
<p>Until that design and data infrastructure matures, some substrate decisions will continue to depend on incomplete models followed by physical test vehicles and qualification.</p>
<p><strong>Conclusion: No single successor</strong><br />
The temptation is to turn every substrate discussion into a succession story. Organic substrates dominated one generation, silicon interposers enabled another, and glass or panel-level technologies are positioned as the next replacement. The actual development path is becoming messier because each solution removes a constraint while introducing another.</p>
<p>Glass can provide dimensional stability and support large formats, but it brings new TGV, adhesion, handling, chipping, and cracking problems. Organic substrates retain mature infrastructure and cost advantages, while finer routing, additional layers, and embedded functions continue to challenge what they can do. Bridges and fan-out approaches can reduce dependence on large silicon interposers, but they bring their own process-control and yield issues. And none of those choices optimizes power, bandwidth, thermal behavior, reliability, cost, and manufacturability for every application at once.</p>
<p>The more consequential shift is that substrate selection is moving closer to the beginning of system architecture. Package designers increasingly have to decide what the substrate must carry, how fine the wiring needs to be, what materials can survive the process, what the supplier can yield, and how all of that will be modeled and qualified before the package is locked down.</p>
<p>As heterogeneous integration pulls more of the electrical, mechanical, and even optical system into the package, the substrate underneath it becomes harder to separate from the architecture it supports. The industry is no longer converging on one substrate to rule them all. It is learning how many different substrates it is soon going to need.</p>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Researchers at the TU Munich, University of Modena and Reggio Emilia, and Applied Materials published a technical paper titled “System-Technology Co-Evaluation of A7 CFET and A10 NSFET Technologies from Cell Parasitics to Chip Reliability.” Abstract Excerpt: “ In this work, we present a physics-based thermal- and aging-aware system-technology co-evaluation (STCO) flow to assess parasitic RCs in... <a class="read_more" href="https://semiengineering.com/comparing-a7-cfet-and-a10-nanosheet-fets-from-parasitics-to-chip-reliability-tum-unimore-applied-materials/">&#187; read more</a></p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/comparing-a7-cfet-and-a10-nanosheet-fets-from-parasitics-to-chip-reliability-tum-unimore-applied-materials/">Comparing A7 CFET and A10 Nanosheet FETs From Parasitics to Chip Reliability (TUM, UNIMORE, Applied Materials)</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Researchers at the TU Munich, University of Modena and Reggio Emilia, and Applied Materials published a technical paper titled “System-Technology Co-Evaluation of A7 CFET and A10 NSFET Technologies from Cell Parasitics to Chip Reliability.”</p>
<p><strong>Abstract Excerpt:</strong> “ In this work, we present a physics-based thermal- and aging-aware system-technology co-evaluation (STCO) flow to assess parasitic RCs in A7 CFET and A10 NSFET technology nodes. Our flow links calibrated device models, optimized standard-cell generation, automated GDS-to-TCAD conversion enabling accurate 3D parasitic RC extraction, full RTL-to-GDS implementation for an AI accelerator, multiphysics thermal analysis, and physics-based bias temperature instability (BTI) aging evaluation. Using the same device model for both technologies, we can isolate the impact of parasitic RCs and design at different levels of the design flow. ”</p>
<p>Find the <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15326">technical paper here</a>. September 2026.</p>
<p>Benkhelifa, Mahdi, Leon Mayr, Hadi Nour Eddine, Andrea Padovani, Luca Larcher, and Hussam Amrouch. &#8220;System-Technology Co-Evaluation of A7 CFET and A10 NSFET Technologies from Cell Parasitics to Chip Reliability.&#8221; <i>arXiv preprint arXiv:2609.15326</i> (2026).</p>
<p>&nbsp;</p>
<p>&nbsp;</p>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>AI agents move deeper into chip design; China doubles down on AI compute and memory; chip supply chains tighten for equipment and critical materials; TSMC partners accelerate; ICs head to space; optics advances, neural super resolution, auto PQC; Purdue-UIUC workforce training.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/chip-industry-week-in-review-157/">Chip Industry Week In Review</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<h3><strong>AI moves deeper into chip design</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>Cadence </strong>released a <a href="https://newsroom.cadence.com/press-releases/press-release-details/2026/Cadence-Expands-ChipStack-AI-Super-Agent-with-a-New-Agent-for-RTL-Generation-and-Early-PPA-Optimization/default.aspx">new agent for spec-to-RTL generation</a> and early PPA optimization as part of its ChipStack AI Super Agent, reporting about 24% lower area and 18% lower power versus pure foundation model code generation.</li>
<li>The release is part of a broader move toward <a href="https://semiengineering.com/when-ai-agents-cross-chip-design-silos/">specialized AI agents across chip-design workflows</a>, which is creating new challenges around orchestration, integration and guardrails. It&#8217;s also putting more emphasis on <a href="https://semiengineering.com/edas-future-is-evidence-driven-automation/">evidence-driven automation</a>, where AI-generated results still need to be verified before sign-off.</li>
</ul>
<h3><strong>AI innovations</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>Alibaba</strong> unveiled its Zhenwu V900 <a href="https://www.alibabacloud.com/en/press-room/alibaba-unveils-roadmap-on-full-stack-ai-strategy?_p_lc=1&amp;">AI accelerator</a>, with 216GB of memory and 1,200GB/s inter-chip bandwidth. Alibaba says the chip delivers 3× the performance of its M890 predecessor, with mass production planned for Q1 2027. The launch expands China’s domestic options for large-scale AI training and inference amid tighter access to leading U.S. chips.</li>
<li><strong>Imagination</strong> published the first <a href="https://www.imaginationtech.com/news/significant-performance-gains-reinforce-imaginations-gpu-first-strategy/">performance data for its E-Series GPU IP</a> and introduced Neural Super Resolution, combining graphics, compute and AI on one programmable architecture.</li>
</ul>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24281979" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-24-at-10.01.00-PM.png?resize=1754%2C442&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="1754" height="442" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-24-at-10.01.00-PM.png?w=1754&amp;ssl=1 1754w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-24-at-10.01.00-PM.png?resize=300%2C76&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-24-at-10.01.00-PM.png?resize=1024%2C258&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-24-at-10.01.00-PM.png?resize=768%2C194&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-24-at-10.01.00-PM.png?resize=1536%2C387&amp;ssl=1 1536w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-24-at-10.01.00-PM.png?resize=600%2C151&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><br />
<strong>Fig. 1: Schematic of accelerator archipelago vs. converged GPU. Source: Imagination Technologies</strong></p>
<h3><strong>Memory</strong></h3>
<p><strong>China expands memory ambitions</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><strong data-start="751" data-end="759">CXMT</strong> announced that its <a class="decorated-link" href="https://www.cxmt.com/en/news/info_22.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com" target="_new" rel="noopener" data-start="779" data-end="852">fifth-gen G5 DRAM technology</a> entered mass production, along with a new LPDDR5X product line. The company says the process reaches an 11.95nm active-area half-pitch and yields at least 50% more dies per wafer than its previous generation, though it did not disclose actual manufacturing yields.</li>
<li>CXMT is also <a class="decorated-link" href="https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/chinas-cxmt-eyes-flash-memory-push-amid-global-shortage-firm-take-samsung-ymtc-2026-09-18/?utm_source=chatgpt.com" target="_new" rel="noopener" data-start="468" data-end="652">preparing an R&amp;D production line for NAND flash</a> in Beijing, according to Reuters, potentially expanding the DRAM maker into a market led domestically by YMTC.</li>
<li>
<div class="" data-turn-id-container="d457e3ca-9a46-4c8e-a649-c5462596c147" data-is-intersecting="true"><strong data-start="2623" data-end="2631">YMTC</strong> reportedly could begin <a class="decorated-link" href="https://ww2.money-link.com.tw/realtimenews/NewsContent.aspx?PU=1002&amp;SN=6311199001&amp;utm_source=chatgpt.com" target="_new" rel="noopener" data-start="2655" data-end="2784">LPDDR5 trial production as early as year-end</a>, expanding the NAND maker into DRAM as the two Chinese memory companies move into each other’s traditional markets.</div>
<div class="" data-turn-id-container="request-6ab1a73e-b860-83e8-8a4d-a7abb3887d6b-54" data-is-intersecting="true">
<section class="text-token-text-primary w-full focus:outline-none has-data-writing-block:pointer-events-none [&amp;:has([data-writing-block])&gt;*]:pointer-events-auto R6Vx5W_threadScrollVars scroll-mb-[calc(var(--scroll-root-safe-area-inset-bottom,0px)+var(--thread-response-height))] scroll-mt-[calc(var(--header-height)+min(200px,max(70px,20svh)))]" dir="auto" data-turn-id="request-6ab1a73e-b860-83e8-8a4d-a7abb3887d6b-54" data-turn-id-container="request-6ab1a73e-b860-83e8-8a4d-a7abb3887d6b-54" data-testid="conversation-turn-84" data-turn="assistant">
