</div>
</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>HBM and AI memory</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><strong data-start="956" data-end="1030">Samsung</strong> reportedly plans to <a href="https://en.sedaily.com/finance/2026/09/20/samsung-to-double-hbm4-output-next-year-sources-say">at least double HBM4-family</a> output in 2027, according to Seoul Economic Daily.</li>
<li class="p1"><strong>GUC</strong> said its <a href="https://www.guc-asic.com/en/news/PressReleases/PR_20260922">HBM4E PHY and controller</a> are design-ready on TSMC N2P and have already been adopted in customer AI ASICs.</li>
<li><strong data-start="632" data-end="640">Imec</strong> researchers modeled a <a class="decorated-link" href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24343?utm_source=chatgpt.com" target="_new" rel="noopener" data-start="663" data-end="726">3D DRAM-on-GPU architecture</a> with vertically oriented DRAM dies and cooling cavities. Simulations cut peak temperature from 121.7°C to 103.4°C versus an HBM-on-GPU baseline, while bandwidth scaled with active DRAM dies.</li>
</ul>
<h3><strong>Chip policy and supply chains</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>SIA</strong> says China is targeting 80% chip self-sufficiency by 2030, requiring chipmakers to use at least 50% domestic semiconductor manufacturing equipment and giving qualifying domestic products a 20% price advantage in government procurement. <a href="https://www.semiconductors.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/SIA-Comments-to-USTR-2026-China-WTO-Compliance_FINAL.pdf">SIA urged U.S. officials to address those barriers</a> through negotiations and coordinated action with allies.</li>
<li>Chinese authorities are reviewing the use of <strong>Broadcom</strong> <a href="https://www.ft.com/content/b97dde39-7813-4a51-8176-3699e2a468b1">networking technology in state-controlled data centers</a> in keeping with a push to reduce reliance on foreign technology, reports the Financial Times.</li>
<li>The<strong data-start="549" data-end="577"> US Commerce Department</strong> issued a temporary rule <a class="decorated-link" href="https://media.bis.gov/regulations/federal-register-notices?categories=Proposed+rules,Interim+and+final+rules,Export+Administration+Regulations,National+Security+Industrial+Base+Regulations,Information+and+Communication+Technology+and+Services+Regulations,Chemical+Weapons+Convention+Regulations,Additional+Protocol+Regulations&amp;years=2026" target="_new" rel="noopener" data-start="1074" data-end="1508">restricting stockpiling of polysilicon and its derivatives</a> ahead of new Section 232 import measures, which take effect on Dec. 4.</li>
<li><strong>ASML</strong> is currently selling <a href="https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-22/asml-executive-says-europe-s-biggest-firm-has-no-sales-in-europe">no chipmaking machines in Europe</a>, according to EVP Frank Heemskerk, who cited insufficient investment and a lack of new fabs. He warned that Europe risks falling further behind as the U.S., China, and India expand domestic chip production.</li>
<li><strong>US and Japanese officials</strong> met to discuss <a href="https://www.reuters.com/world/china/us-japanese-officials-discussed-chinas-yttrium-curbs-ahead-trump-xi-meeting-2026-09-24/">yttrium and permanent-magnet supply bottlenecks</a> as Chinese export controls continue to constrain critical-material supplies. Yttrium is used in heat-resistant coatings for chip manufacturing equipment. Chinese customs data showed no U.S.-bound shipments in January, May or June.</li>
</ul>
<h3><strong data-start="363" data-end="390">TSMC ecosystem developments</strong></h3>
<p>At the <strong>TSMC</strong> 2026 North America OIP Ecosystem Forum in Santa Clara, several ecosystem partners announced expanded collaborations:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Siemens</strong> and TSMC introduced an AI agent for <a href="https://news.siemens.com/en-us/siemens-tsmc-oip-ecosystem-forum-2026/">automated design rule check</a> fixing across IC flows.</li>
<li><strong>Synopsys</strong> and TSMC are extending their work across <a href="https://news.synopsys.com/2026-09-23-Synopsys-and-TSMC-Partner-to-Accelerate-AI-Systems-Innovation-with-Agentic-AI-and-Advanced-Design">advanced-node design and packaging</a>, including certified digital and analog EDA flows for TSMC’s A14 process and new agentic AI workflows for analog, digital, and multi-die designs. The companies also extended support for integrated voltage regulators on CoWoS and co-packaged optics.</li>
<li><strong>Cadence</strong> demonstrated a <a href="https://newsroom.cadence.com/press-releases/press-release-details/2026/Cadence-Collaborates-With-TSMC-to-Deliver-Certified-Tool-Solutions-and-Industry-Leading-Silicon-Proven-UALink-IP-on-TSMC-Advanced-Processes/default.aspx">UALink solution in N3P</a>, introduced new Si-proven IP for N3P and N2P, and achieved tool certification for TSMC’s A14 process.</li>
<li><strong>AlChip and Synopsys</strong> demonstrated a <a href="https://www.alchip.com/en/Newsroom/Alchip_Synopsys_TSMC_OIP">224G SerDes implementation</a> for AI accelerators.</li>
<li><strong>IC-Link</strong> by <strong>imec</strong> joined TSMC’s OIP Cloud Alliance to expand customer access to <a href="https://www.imec-int.com/en/press/ic-link-imec-expands-collaboration-tsmc-accelerate-customer-access-advanced-node-chip-design">advanced-node</a> chip design infrastructure and support.</li>
</ul>
<h3><strong>At the leading edge</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>ETH Zurich</strong> researchers created <a href="https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-11042-0">light-emitting photoresists</a> that can be patterned with UV or electron beams, producing fluorescent features down to 110 nm and OLEDs with 13.3% peak EQE.</li>
<li><strong>Carnegie Mellon</strong>-led researchers fabricated <a href="https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-026-77186-9">wafer-scale monolayer MoS₂ transistors</a> with physical channel lengths below 5 nm using CMOS-compatible photolithography.</li>
<li><strong data-start="877" data-end="885">Imec</strong> developed a <a class="decorated-link" href="https://www.imec-int.com/en/press/imec-debuts-100-ghz-gesi-avalanche-photodiode-apd-enabling-net-400-gbps-data-reception-just-5?utm_source=chatgpt.com" target="_new" rel="noopener" data-start="898" data-end="1063">100 GHz Ge/Si avalanche photodiode</a>, demonstrating what it claims is the first net 400 Gbps optical link using an APD receiver, targeting AI data-center interconnects.</li>
<li><strong data-start="132" data-end="146">Infleqtion</strong> demonstrated <a class="decorated-link" href="https://infleqtion.com/demonstration-of-30-logical-qubits-on-sqale/" target="_new" rel="noopener" data-start="160" data-end="258">30 entangled logical qubits</a> using 80 physical neutral-atom qubits on its Sqale QPU, with a distance-2 code that detects errors and corrects atom loss.</li>
</ul>
<h3><strong>Noteworthy deals and funding</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>RealSense</strong>, the <a href="https://investor.cognex.com/news/news-details/2026/Cognex-to-Acquire-RealSense-Expanding-Machine-Vision-Leadership-into-High-Growth-Robotic-Perception-Market/default.aspx">former Intel depth-sensing and 3D-vision</a> business, will be acquired by <strong>Cognex</strong> for $500M, expanding its reach into robotic perception and physical AI.</li>
<li><strong>Qualcomm</strong> agreed to acquire <strong>PickNik</strong>, developer and steward of the open-source MoveIt <a href="https://www.qualcomm.com/news/releases/2026/09/qualcomm-to-acquire-picknik-to-advance-the-future-of-open-roboti">robotics-manipulation</a> framework.</li>
<li><strong>PicoJool</strong> raised $27.5M to commercialize its 200G <a href="https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260922057600/en/PicoJool-Raises-%2427.5-Million-Series-A-to-Scale-Optical-Connectivity-for-AI-Infrastructure">VCSEL and MicroVCSEL</a> technology for AI optical interconnects.</li>
</ul>

<h2 id="Global"><strong>Global</strong></h2>
<h3><strong>Europe</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>Arm</strong> joined the <a href="https://newsroom.arm.com/blog/arm-joins-eurocdp-europe-chip-innovation">European Chips Design Platform</a> as its first commercial IP provider, giving European startups, SMEs, and research teams access to Arm IP, tools, training, and design support through Arm Flexible Access.</li>
<li><strong>Germany</strong>’s <strong>SPRIND</strong> and the <strong>Netherlands</strong>’ <strong>NADI</strong> launched a 20-month <a href="https://www.sprind.org/en/actions/challenges/ai-native-chip-design">competition aimed at using AI</a> for architecture search, RTL generation and verification to shorten chip-development cycles from years to weeks.</li>
<li>In <strong>Switzerland</strong>,<strong> SEALSQ</strong>, and <strong>WISeKey </strong>plan to establish a <a href="https://www.sealsq.com/investors/news-releases/sealsq-wisekey-and-canton-of-jura-sign-mou-to-establish-a-swiss-post-quantum-semiconductor-and-cybersecurity-center">Post-Quantum Semiconductor and Cybersecurity</a> Center in the <strong>Canton of Jura</strong>.</li>
</ul>
<h3><strong>Asia</strong></h3>
<div class="Wl_3jG_Trigger" tabindex="0" role="button" data-d-component="popover-trigger" data-d-inline-text="" aria-haspopup="dialog" aria-expanded="false" data-state="closed">
<ul>
<li><strong>Taiwan</strong> broke ground on the <a href="https://investtaiwan.nat.gov.tw/newsPage99132cht">Baipu Industrial Park</a> in Kaohsiung, which will include the country’s first testing and validation base dedicated to advanced semiconductor equipment and materials.</li>
<li><strong>Thailand</strong> approved its first <a href="https://www.boi.go.th/index.php?page=press_releases_detail&amp;topic_id=139424&amp;_module=news&amp;from_page=press_releases2">national semiconductor and advanced electronics strategy</a>, targeting about $80B in cumulative investment and $150B in annual industry revenue by 2050.</li>
</ul>

<h2 id="Reports and Deals"><strong>Reports and Deals</strong></h2>
<h3><strong>More deals and partnerships</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>AT&amp;S</strong> and <strong>Marvell</strong> signed a deal to increase <a href="https://ats.net/en/press/ats-and-marvell-technology-expand-collaboration-to-support-next-generation-ai-infrastructure">advanced IC substrate capacity</a> for AI and cloud infrastructure.</li>
<li><strong>SMART Photonics </strong>and <strong>GF </strong>are developing an <a href="https://www.smartphotonics.nl/knowledge-hub/smart-photonics-partners-with-globalfoundries">open-access foundry service</a> that combines GF silicon photonics with SMART Photonics’ indium-phosphide lasers and optical amplifiers.</li>
<li><strong>GS Micro</strong> and <strong>Teradyne</strong> formed a <a href="https://www.gsme.com/news-updates/gsme-and-teradyne-announce-their-partnership">multi-year partnership</a> to establish a semiconductor test and evaluation center at GSME’s new Silicon Valley headquarters.</li>
<li><strong>proteanTecs</strong> and <strong>GUC</strong> are bringing <a href="https://www.proteantecs.com/pressroom/proteantecs-and-guc-expand-collaboration-to-provide-lifecycle-health-and-performance-monitoring-for-custom-socs">embedded health and performance monitoring</a> into GUC custom SoCs, extending earlier work around die-to-die links, HBM subsystems, and advanced packaging into the compute fabric itself.</li>
<li><strong>NLM Photonics</strong> and <strong>SilOriX</strong> inked a <a href="https://www.nlmphotonics.com/2026/09/21/nlm-photonics-and-silorix-enter-into-joint-development-agreement">joint PIC development agreement</a>.</li>
</ul>
<h3><strong>Fundings</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>Nexstrom</strong> raised $12M to commercialize a <a href="https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/nexstrom-raises-12-million-seed-round-to-commercialize-the-first-12-inch-single-crystal-2d-semiconductor-platform-302885862.html">300mm single-crystal 2D semiconductor platform</a>.</li>
<li><strong>MetaOptics</strong> secured an investment facility of up to $10M to expand in the U.S. and build a 300mm production line for <a href="https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/metaoptics-secures-up-to-us10-million-investment-facility-from-white-lion-capital-its-first-us-institutional-investor-to-onshore-metalens-technology-into-the-us-302884152.html">metalenses used in optical</a> interconnects, lidar and consumer devices.</li>
</ul>
<h3><strong>Market forecasts</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>Yole</strong> expects the <a href="https://www.yolegroup.com/press-release/high-end-packaging-a-market-set-to-nearly-quintuple-by-2031/">high-end packaging market</a> to grow nearly fivefold to more than $51B by 2031, with AI infrastructure driving demand for technologies including hybrid bonding, CoWoS-L and CPO.</li>
<li><strong>McKinsey</strong> raised its 2030 <a href="https://www.mckinsey.com/industries/semiconductors/our-insights/the-2-point-3-trillion-dollar-horizon-how-ai-is-rewriting-the-semiconductor-story">semiconductor market forecast to $2.3T</a>, up 44% from its previous $1.6T estimate, with server and data-center chip revenue projected to reach $1.2T by 2030. McKinsey expects supply constraints, particularly for leading-edge chips and HBM, to persist for another 3 to 5 years.</li>
<li>The global <a href="https://www.trendforce.com/presscenter/news/20260922-13249.html">DRAM module market</a> generated $21.2B in 2025, up 59% year over year, reports TrendForce.</li>
</ul>

<li><strong data-start="1128" data-end="1146">Brewer Science</strong> developed a <a class="decorated-link" href="https://www.brewerscience.com/news-imaps-2026/?utm_source=chatgpt.com" target="_new" rel="noopener" data-start="1159" data-end="1248">high-temperature laser-release material</a> for advanced-packaging temporary bonding/debonding.</li>
<li><strong data-start="1496" data-end="1503">ASM</strong> launched <a class="decorated-link" href="https://www.asm.com/our-technology-products/pecvd/asm-flowable-carbon" target="_new" rel="noopener" data-start="1513" data-end="1612">XP8 Vertos Flowable Carbon</a>, a PECVD process that combines gap fill and self-planarization for high-aspect-ratio structures in advanced logic, DRAM and 3D NAND.</li>
<li><strong>Cognex</strong> introduced an AI-based <a href="https://www.cognex.com/en/company/press-releases/in-sight-1750-press-release">wafer and panel identification</a> system for semiconductor manufacturing.</li>

<h2 id="Research"><strong>Research</strong></h2>
<p><strong>WashU</strong> researchers and collaborators demonstrated <a href="https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-11000-w">heterogeneous photonic integration of single-crystalline nanomembranes</a> on silicon and silicon nitride.</p>
<div class="ANObbW_Badge lKEGNW_Badge" data-color="secondary" data-size="sm" data-pill="" data-variant="soft" data-d-component="badge" data-d-hoverable="" data-d-weight="normal">
<div class="oIb9lq_Box" data-d-auto-spacing="" data-d-component="row" data-d-direction="row">
<div class="oIb9lq_Box QGyuMa_FaviconBox" role="presentation" data-d-auto-spacing="" data-d-component="favicon" data-d-direction="col" data-d-has-width="" data-d-has-height="">
<p>A <strong>LANL</strong>/<strong>University of Pisa</strong>-led team reviewed how <a href="https://www.nature.com/articles/s42254-026-00978-x">self-organizing networks of nanowires and nanoparticles</a> adapt their electrical connections to process information and learn directly in HW. The approach could complement conventional computing by enabling energy-efficient, local AI in robots, autonomous vehicles and satellites. &#8220;We&#8217;re asking what becomes possible when the hardware itself is adaptive,&#8221;<a href="https://www.chemistry.ucla.edu/news/ucla-researchers-advance-physical-ai/"> said</a> co-author Adam Stieg of <strong>UCLA</strong>, pointing to AI that can operate and adapt locally.</p>
<p><strong>Keysight</strong> is supporting <strong>UC Berkeley</strong> research on new <a href="http://keysight.com/us/en/about/newsroom/catalog/news-release.2026.0924-pr26-089-keysight-enables-uc-berkeley-research-to-advance-6g-over-the-air-testing.html">over-the-air test methods for increasingly complex 6G</a> devices and systems.</p>

<h2 id="Security"><strong>Security</strong></h2>
<h3><strong>Hardware and firmware </strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>CERT/CC</strong> warned that <a href="https://www.kb.cert.org/vuls/id/738147">vendor-signed UEFI Shell applications</a> from multiple hardware vendors can be used to bypass Secure Boot and execute untrusted code before the operating system loads.</li>
</ul>
<h3><strong>AI and cybercrime</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li>An <strong>OpenAI</strong> agent accessed <a href="https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-09-24/openai-agents-plotted-to-access-data-amid-medicare-hack/107189504">non-public files on an Australian Medicare statistics portal</a> while performing an internal research task. Separately, researchers found evidence of multiple OpenAI agents coordinating attempts to access data from several Australian government sites.</li>
<li>Meanwhile, OpenAI called for <a href="https://openai.com/index/building-standards-next-phase-ai/">international technical standards</a> for frontier AI covering capability evaluation, human oversight, incident reporting, and automated AI research.</li>
<li><strong>Microsoft</strong> <a href="https://blogs.microsoft.com/on-the-issues/2026/09/22/disrupting-eviltokens-the-ai-chatbot-built-for-cybercrime/">disrupted EvilTokens</a>, an AI-enabled cybercrime service linked to more than 12,000 compromised inboxes at over 10,000 organizations. Microsoft and its partners seized 50 websites and disabled more than 150 related domains.</li>
<li><strong>Palo Alto Networks</strong> launched an <a href="https://investors.paloaltonetworks.com/news-releases/news-release-details/palo-alto-networks-delivers-anthropics-mythos-and-openais-gpt-56">agentic offensive-security service</a> that uses Anthropic and OpenAI cyber models to continuously identify, validate, and help remediate exploitable attack paths.</li>
</ul>
<h3><strong>Alerts</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li>A hacking group <a href="https://www.404media.co/we-hacked-the-fbi-hackers-say-they-have-data-on-all-fbi-employees/">claims it breached the FBI</a>, stealing sensitive data, including FBI agents’ names, addresses, phone numbers, and information on their spouses. The FBI said it is “<a href="https://x.com/FBI/status/2102807819695071709">actively and aggressively investigating</a>” the incident.</li>
<li><strong>CISA</strong> released <a href="https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/USDHSCISA/bulletins/42bfaa9">nine industrial control systems advisories</a> this week. All the agency’s alerts for this week are <a href="https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories">here</a>.</li>
<li><strong>ENISA</strong> said cyber dependencies and supply-chain exposure are expanding the EU’s attack surface, with manufacturing accounting for 7% of recorded incidents. Its <a href="https://www.enisa.europa.eu/news/exploring-the-evolution-of-the-cyber-threat-landscape-how-dependencies-weaken-our-digital-resilience">2026 Threat Landscape</a> also found more than 48,000 new CVEs in 2025, up 22%, and warned that AI is increasingly being used to support malicious operations.</li>
</ul>

<h2 id="Vehicles, Batteries"><strong>Vehicles, Batteries</strong></h2>
<h3><strong>Automotive Deals &amp; Products</strong></h3>
</div>

In benchmarks simulating up to 408 logical qubits and more than 31.5M operations, the decoder added as little as 0.02% delay, according to IonQ.</p>
<p>In Germany, <strong>QUDORA</strong> will lead a 7-member consortium that has been <a href="https://qudora.com/news/german-government-selects-qudora-led-consortium-for-e122-million-project-nfqc-1k-to-develop-a-1000-qubit-fault-tolerant-quantum-computer-and-build-a-qpu-pilot-line/">invited to submit a full proposal</a> for NFQC-1k, a roughly €122 million project to build a trapped-ion quantum computer with at least 1,000 physical and 50 logical qubits, plus a QPU pilot manufacturing line.</p>

		<title>A Network-on-Chip (NoC) For Multi-Die Devices</title>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Transporting the native packetized traffic of the NoC directly across die boundaries using a stable, invariant interface.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/a-network-on-chip-noc-for-multi-die-devices/">A Network-on-Chip (NoC) For Multi-Die Devices</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>The semiconductor industry is rapidly transitioning from monolithic SoCs to chiplet-based architectures. At the same time, AI workloads are evolving beyond cloud inference into physical AI: systems that perceive, reason, and act in the real world. Autonomous vehicles, industrial robots, humanoid robots, drones, and intelligent manufacturing systems all require continuous, high-volume data flow between heterogeneous compute engines.</p>
<p>However, these two trends expose a weakness in today’s die-to-die communication architectures. While coherent interconnect protocols have been highly successful for processor-centric systems, they are fundamentally mismatched to the traffic patterns generated by modern AI accelerators.</p>
<p>As a result, a new approach is needed that involves transporting the native packetized traffic of the NoC directly across die boundaries using a stable, invariant interface.</p>
<h2>Physical AI changes the nature of on-chip communication</h2>
<p>Traditional processors are dominated by memory accesses, synchronization, and cache coherence. Physical AI systems are different. A modern automotive compute platform may simultaneously execute:</p>
<ul>
<li>Multiple camera processing pipelines</li>
<li>Radar and lidar signal processing</li>
<li>Sensor fusion</li>
<li>AI perception networks</li>
<li>Localization and mapping</li>
<li>Path planning</li>
<li>Functional safety monitoring</li>
<li>Vehicle actuator control</li>
</ul>
<p>Rather than exchanging individual cache lines, these engines often exchange continuous streams of feature maps, tensors, point clouds, video frames, and intermediate inference results. These data streams often consist of hundreds of kilobytes, or even megabytes, moving between specialized accelerators at deterministic rates. The communication pattern resembles a high-performance dataflow network more than a coherent symmetric multi-processor system. As physical AI systems become more capable, the amount of accelerator-to-accelerator traffic continues to grow faster than CPU-to-memory traffic.</p>
<h2>Where coherent protocols excel</h2>
<p>Coherent die-to-die protocols remain the right solution for many applications and perform exceptionally well for:</p>
<ul>
<li>Coherent communication between processor dies in large SMP systems</li>
<li>CPU memory accesses</li>
<li>Synchronization</li>
<li>Control-plane communication from CPUs to I/O management processors or accelerators</li>
</ul>
<p>These protocols were designed to maintain memory consistency while moving relatively small cache-line-sized transactions. For processor-centric workloads sharing memory, they are extremely effective.</p>
<h2>Why are they inefficient for AI data movement?</h2>
<p>Accelerator traffic follows very different patterns. Most coherent protocols divide communication into cache-line-sized transactions, typically 64 bytes each. Every cache line carries protocol overhead, including:</p>
<ul>
<li>Addresses</li>
<li>Transaction identifiers</li>
<li>Ordering information</li>
<li>Response tracking</li>
<li>Coherence metadata</li>
</ul>
<p>When transferring large tensors or feature maps, this overhead must be repeated thousands of times. For AI workloads, the actual payload accounts for only a portion of the transmitted bandwidth, with protocol overhead consuming an increasingly significant fraction of the available die-to-die bandwidth.</p>
<p>Some coherent protocols have added optimizations to help improve the efficiency of non-coherent, bursty traffic. While useful, these mechanisms are limited in scope. For example, they span only a small number of beats and cannot fully ameliorate the overhead associated with very long streaming transfers of arbitrary data. As accelerator bandwidth increases into the terabytes-per-second range inside future automotive AI systems, repeatedly transmitting cache-line metadata becomes increasingly difficult to justify.</p>
<h2>Existing approaches</h2>
<p>Many non-coherent die-to-die approaches have been proposed, including:</p>
<ul>
<li>AMD/Xilinx AXI Chip2Chip, which is deployed in FPGA implementations.</li>
<li>Open Chiplet Atlas (OCA) AXI over UCIe (AoU), a proposal from Tenstorrent/OCA.</li>
<li>Various proprietary approaches that serialize AXI over high-speed serial interfaces.</li>
</ul>
<p>These approaches extend AXI interfaces across die boundaries and work well for connecting peripherals and control-oriented IP. However, they still operate at the transaction layer. Each NoC packet of each virtual channel must be converted into AXI transactions before crossing the die boundary, then reconstructed as NoC packets on the receiving side. As systems scale to dozens of AI engines across multiple chiplets, this repeated conversion adds unnecessary latency, buffering, and implementation complexity.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24281897" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Arteris_NoC-for-Multi-Die-Devices-fig1-scaled.webp?resize=2560%2C1273&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="2560" height="1273" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Arteris_NoC-for-Multi-Die-Devices-fig1-scaled.webp?w=2560&amp;ssl=1 2560w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Arteris_NoC-for-Multi-Die-Devices-fig1-scaled.webp?resize=300%2C149&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Arteris_NoC-for-Multi-Die-Devices-fig1-scaled.webp?resize=1024%2C509&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Arteris_NoC-for-Multi-Die-Devices-fig1-scaled.webp?resize=768%2C382&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Arteris_NoC-for-Multi-Die-Devices-fig1-scaled.webp?resize=1536%2C764&amp;ssl=1 1536w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Arteris_NoC-for-Multi-Die-Devices-fig1-scaled.webp?resize=2048%2C1019&amp;ssl=1 2048w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Arteris_NoC-for-Multi-Die-Devices-fig1-scaled.webp?resize=600%2C298&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /></p>
<p><strong>Fig. 1: Multi-die interconnect in physical AI applications. Source: </strong><a href="https://bit.ly/3KcLBOH"><strong>Arteris, Inc</strong></a><strong>.</strong></p>
<h2>Direct NoC-to-NoC communication</h2>
<p>A more natural architecture is to allow the NoC itself to span multiple dies. Instead of terminating the NoC at each chiplet boundary, native NoC packets are transported directly across the die-to-die interface. The remote die simply becomes another portion of the same logical network. This provides several important advantages:</p>
<ul>
<li>Streaming transfers remain packetized from producer to consumer without being repeatedly converted into cache-line transactions and AXI interfaces. Protocol overhead is amortized across long data streams rather than repeated for every cache line.</li>
<li>Virtual channels enable multiple traffic classes, including control traffic, real-time sensor data, AI inference traffic, and bulk DMA transfers, to share the same physical die-to-die connection while maintaining quality of service (QoS).</li>
<li>Existing NoC routing, arbitration, congestion management, and QoS mechanisms naturally extend across multiple dies.</li>
<li>Multiple protocols can be transported over the same die-to-die interface: for example, AXI, APB, AHB or OCP.</li>
<li>Most importantly, the die boundary ceases to be a protocol translation point. It simply becomes an additional hop in a single, multi-die network-on-chip.</li>
</ul>
<h2>Why does this matter for automotive physical AI?</h2>
<p>Automotive AI places unique demands on interconnects. Unlike cloud AI systems, automotive platforms must satisfy strict latency, determinism, power, and functional safety requirements while operating within tight thermal limits. Centralized vehicle compute platforms will integrate multiple AI chiplets connected through advanced packaging technologies. Individual chiplets may specialize in:</p>
<ul>
<li>Vision processing</li>
<li>Neural network inference</li>
<li>Radar processing</li>
<li>Lidar processing</li>
<li>CPU clusters</li>
<li>Safety and security islands</li>
<li>Memory expansion</li>
<li>Networking</li>
</ul>
<p>The largest traffic flows are often not between CPUs and memory but between accelerators themselves. For example:</p>
<ul>
<li>Camera processing → AI perception → Sensor fusion → Planning → Vehicle control</li>
<li>Shared tensor movement between multiple neural-network accelerators</li>
</ul>
<p>These are fundamentally streaming dataflow applications. Transporting these streams using a native packetized NoC enables far more efficient bandwidth utilization, while reducing latency and buffering throughout the system. The result is higher sustained throughput, lower energy consumption per transferred bit, and greater scalability as additional accelerator chiplets are added.</p>
<h2>The challenge of exposing internal NoC protocols</h2>
<p>Despite these advantages, directly exposing an implementation’s internal NoC protocol is problematic. Internal packet formats frequently evolve as NoC implementations gain new capabilities, such as:</p>
<ul>
<li>Improved routing algorithms</li>
<li>New arbitration policies</li>
<li>Additional virtual channels</li>
<li>Enhanced QoS mechanisms</li>
<li>Updated packet formats</li>
</ul>
<p>Even relatively small NoC changes can significantly alter the internal protocol, making long-term die-to-die compatibility challenging. Routing introduces another challenge. Packet routing information may depend on the topology of the destination NoC. If the topology changes, routing vectors or addressing schemes may need to be updated. Without architectural stability, every NoC revision risks requiring die-to-die interface updates. While this may be manageable when a single team designs all dies, it becomes impractical when teams work independently.</p>
<h2>An invariant NoC interface</h2>
<p>The solution is to define an invariant architectural interface, rather than exposing the evolving internal NoC implementation. An invariant, die-to-die NoC interface provides a stable packet protocol specifically designed for die-to-die transport while allowing each chiplet’s internal NoC implementation to continue evolving independently.</p>
<p>Such an interface can:</p>
<ul>
<li>Support multiple non-coherent protocols over a single NoC transport layer.</li>
<li>Define a stable packet format.</li>
<li>Support configurable interface widths to scale bandwidth.</li>
<li>Support virtual channels for multiple traffic classes.</li>
<li>Preserve NoC routing semantics while abstracting implementation details.</li>
<li>Isolate future NoC enhancements from the die-to-die interface.</li>
<li>Facilitate a choice of physical layer implementation: for example, UCIe, BoW, PCIe or a vendor-specific PHY.</li>
</ul>
<p>This enables chiplets from different product generations to communicate through a stable architectural interface, while allowing incremental change on either side of the die-to-die boundary.</p>
<h2>Efficiency and scalability for future AI systems</h2>
<p>We propose a multi-die NoC packet transport interface based on an invariant die-to-die NoC interface. Instead of transporting cache-line transactions or extending AXI buses, the interface carries native, protocol-independent NoC packets directly between chiplets using a stable, implementation-independent packet format. The interface can be sized to match the bandwidth requirements of future AI systems, supports virtual channels for efficient sharing among diverse traffic types, and extends NoC routing seamlessly across die boundaries.</p>
<p>For physical AI, particularly in next-generation automotive computing platforms, this approach aligns the communication architecture with the system&#8217;s dominant traffic pattern: high-bandwidth, low-latency accelerator-to-accelerator data movement. By eliminating unnecessary protocol translation and minimizing transaction overhead, it creates a scalable, multi-protocol, multi-die interconnect capable of supporting increasingly complex AI pipelines, while maintaining the determinism, efficiency, and long-term architectural stability required for safety-critical deployments.</p>
<p>Learn more about <a href="https://hubs.ly/Q03sxzTc0">Arteris’ multi-die solution</a>.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/a-network-on-chip-noc-for-multi-die-devices/">A Network-on-Chip (NoC) For Multi-Die Devices</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></content:encoded>
